subject: religious-studies
title: Analogy, Symbol, and Myth
welcome_lead: Listen as Aquinas, Tillich, and Bultmann tune three different instruments to play the music of God-talk.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on analogy (Aquinas), symbol (Tillich), and demythologisation (Bultmann).
final_note: Cognitive and non-cognitive theories agree on at least this: God-talk cannot be merely literal.

concepts.def: Language used in exactly the same sense in two contexts; Aquinas denies our terms for God are merely univocal.
Language used in entirely different senses; Aquinas denies our terms for God are merely equivocal.
Aquinas' use of analogy where the primary instance (God) is the source of the perfection in creatures (e.g. 'God is good' as cause of all goodness).
Aquinas' use of analogy where a property is predicated proportionately to the nature of each being (e.g. divine goodness proportionate to divine nature).

Rudolf Bultmann's project of reinterpreting the mythological language of the New Testament in existentialist categories.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Aquinas (Summa Theologica, I, q. 13) holds that our language for God is neither univocal (we are not gods) nor wholly equivocal (we can still say true things about God).

It is analogical: terms like 'wise' and 'good' apply to God and creatures in related but proportionate senses, grounded in the causal relation between Creator and creature.

Paul Tillich's Dynamics of Faith (1957) distinguishes signs (arbitrary pointers) from symbols (which participate in what they signify).

Religious symbols, including 'God' itself as the symbol of the Ultimate, open up levels of reality and of the soul that no literal language can reach. Only the statement 'God is being-itself' is non-symbolic.

Rudolf Bultmann's New Testament and Mythology (1941) argues that the New Testament's three-storey cosmology and miracle accounts are mythological expressions of the early Church's existential encounter with God in Christ.

The task of theology is to demythologise: to translate this mythological language into existentialist categories of authentic existence.

mcqs.q: How did Hume define a miracle?
options: Hume believed all miracles in the Bible really happened.
Hume defined a miracle as something amazing or unexpected.
A violation of the laws of nature by a particular volition of the Deity — and he argued evidence for such violations could never outweigh the uniform experience supporting the laws.
